# Activity

Given that camera traps operate 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and can record animal motion down to second-level precision, they represent a powerful tool to explore and contrast the activity patterns of the species they detect! Such analyses can give insight into competition, predation and coexistence. Characterizing the "activity level" - the proportion of the day which animals are active - is also increasingly important for new estimators of animal density ([see the density chapter for more info](#density)). Consequently, understanding how to derive and use activity data is very important for people using camera traps.

*Must read* [Frey, Sandra, et al. "Investigating animal activity patterns and temporal niche partitioning using camera‐trap data: Challenges and opportunities." Remote Sensing in Ecology and Conservation 3.3 (2017): 123-132.](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/rse2.60)

Two key packages

-   `overlap` <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/overlap/index.html>
-   `activity` <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/activity/index.html>

They each use the timestamps in camera trap detetions to derive activity indices which can be compared between different strata of interest (e.g. species, treatments etc.).

Here we will use the `activity` package.

## Independent detections or raw data?

A recent paper has highlighted that we need to carefully consider our data source for activity analyses:

[Christopher Peral, Marietjie Landman, Graham I. H. Kerley The inappropriate use of time-to-independence biases estimates of activity patterns of free-ranging mammals derived from camera traps Ecology and Evolution](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ece3.9408?af=R)

Whilst we typically use "independent data" for most of our camera trap analysis, doing so may throw away useful data on activity. Both in terms of the number of data points (power) but also the activity patterns they generate. Peral et.al show that 70% of papers published to date use independent data to derive their indices. They actually state:**"We conclude that the application of time-to-independence data filters in camera trap-based estimates of activity patterns is not valid and should not be used."**

So we will use the raw data to derive our indices!

**Load your packages**

```{r ch9_1, echo=T, results='hide', message =F, warning=F, class.source="Rmain"}
# Check you have them and load them
list.of.packages <- c("kableExtra", "tidyr", "ggplot2", "gridExtra", "activity", "overlap", "dplyr","lubridate" )

new.packages <- list.of.packages[!(list.of.packages %in% installed.packages()[,"Package"])]
if(length(new.packages)) install.packages(new.packages)
lapply(list.of.packages, require, character.only = TRUE)

```

## Data formatting

First, let's import the processed raw data file.

```{r ch9_2, class.source="Rmain"}
# Import the data
img <- read.csv("data/processed_data/AlgarRestorationProject_raw_detections.csv", header=T)
```

Which looks like this:

```{r ch9_3, echo=F}
kbl(head(img))%>%
  kable_paper() %>%
  scroll_box(height = "200px")
```

Then load the activity package:

```{r ch9_4, class.source="Rmain"}
# Load the package
library(activity) 
```

If your cameras correct for daylight savings use the appropriate timezone code, if they do not, use UTC.

```{r ch9_5, results="hide", class.source="Rmain"}
img$timestamp <- ymd_hms(img$timestamp, tz="UTC")
```

Note - find your timezone code for the `tz=` call [here](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones).

### Accounting for sunrise and sunset

A recent paper highlighted the challenges in trying to understand animal activity patterns at high latitudes - as sunrise/sunset timings vary substantially through the calender year. See:

[Vazquez, Carmen, et al. "Comparing diel activity patterns of wildlife across latitudes and seasons: Time transformations using day length." Methods in Ecology and Evolution 10.12 (2019): 2057-2066.](https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.13290)

If we want to compare activity patterns between two different locations, or different seasons, the day length at the time the detection occurred can have a huge impact on our estimates of wildlife activity. For example, if we wanted to compare day/night activity between winter and summer periods, in winter animal activity is constrained to a much shorter day length.

Fortunately, the authors have a solution!

**The average anchoring method**

Instead of using the 'human' 24h clock, we can instead express animal activity relative to an important anchor point in the day (e.g. sunrise).

NOTE -the transformation is not necessary at latitudes below 20°, or in studies with a duration of less than a month (below 40° latitude), as day length doesn't chnage substantially.

```{r ch9_6, class.source="Rmain", results='hide', message =F, warning=F}
# We need to add latitude and longitude to our observations
# import our station locations (and other covariates)
locs <-  read.csv("data/processed_data/AlgarRestorationProject_camera_locations_and_covariates.csv")

# Add them to our data frame
img_locs <- left_join(img, locs)

# calculate solar time 
tmp <- solartime ( img_locs$timestamp, # the date time column 
                   img_locs$latitude,  # Latitude
                   img_locs$longitude, # Longitude
                   tz=-6,              # an offset in numeric hours to UTC (Alberta is 6 hours behind)
                   format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")

# Although we want to use solar time, let's add both incase you want to explore the implications
img_locs$solar <- tmp$solar
img_locs$clock <- tmp$clock

```

Let's check out the relationship between these two indices:

```{r ch9_7, class.source="Rinfo"}
plot(img_locs$clock, img_locs$solar)
```

We are now ready to fit some models!

## Species comparisons

Let's start with a white-tailed deer and caribou example.

Note we are reducing the number of replicates to 100 to speed up the process - typically people use 1000.

```{r ch9_8, class.source="Rmain"}
# Fit an activity model
m1 <- fitact(img_locs$solar[img_locs$sp=="Odocoileus.virginianus"], sample="model", reps=100)
plot(m1)
```

Take a look at the raw data if you want.

```{r ch9_9, eval=FALSE, class.source="Rinfo"}
m1
```

And repeat it for Caribou

```{r ch9_10, class.source="Rmain"}
# Fit an activity model
m2 <- fitact(img_locs$solar[img_locs$sp=="Rangifer.tarandus"], sample="model", reps=100)
plot(m2)
```

We can plot both on the same axis as follows:

```{r ch9_11, class.source="Rmain"}
plot(m2, yunit="density", data="none", las=1, lwd=2,
     tline=list(lwd=2), # Thick line 
     cline=list(lty=0)) # Supress confidence intervals

plot(m1, yunit="density", data="none", add=TRUE, 
     tline=list(col="red", lwd=2),
     cline=list(lty=0))

legend("topright", c("Caribou", "Deer"), col=1:2, lty=1, lwd=2)
```

We can compare different activity patterns using coefficient of overlap (∆) - developed by Ridout and Linkie:

[Ridout, Martin S., and Matthew Linkie. "Estimating overlap of daily activity patterns from camera trap data." Journal of Agricultural, Biological, and Environmental Statistics 14.3 (2009): 322-337.](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1198/jabes.2009.08038)

The coefficient ranges from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (complete overlap). We can implement for a two species comparison as follows:

```{r ch9_12, class.source="Rmain"}
# Note reps reduced to speed up running time - people typically use 1000.
compareCkern(m1, m2, reps = 100)
```

The output above represents:

0 = no overlap and 1 = high overlap!

-   `obs` = observed overlap index;
-   `null` = mean null overlap index;
-   `seNull` = standard error of the null distribution;
-   `pNull` = probability observed index arose by chance. Low pNull means the patterns differ.

The observed overlap (0.78) is lower than we would expect if deer had the same activity pattern on both feature types (0.96), and none of the randomisations produced an overlap this low (pNull=<0.01). This suggests the patterns differ, although they still overlap substantially, so the size of any change looks modest.

## Treatment comparisons

We can also compare patterns within a species across different strata of interest. For example, perhaps white-tailed deer change their activity patterns in response to the `feature_type` they are using - perhaps they will be more nocturnal on `HumanUse` lines relative to `Offline` strata. Lets try it:

**White-tail deer on HumanUse feature**

```{r ch9_13, class.source="Rmain"}
#Fit an activity model
m1 <- fitact(img_locs$solar[img_locs$sp=="Odocoileus.virginianus" &
                              img_locs$feature_type=="HumanUse"], sample="model", reps=100)
```

**White-tail deer on Offline feature**

```{r ch9_14, class.source="Rmain"}
m2 <- fitact(img_locs$solar[img_locs$sp=="Odocoileus.virginianus" &
                              img_locs$feature_type=="Offline"], sample="model", reps=100)
```

Plot the results:

```{r ch9_15, class.source="Rmain"}

plot(m2, yunit="density", data="none", las=1, lwd=2,
     tline=list(lwd=2), # Thick line 
     cline=list(lty=0)) # Supress confidence intervals

plot(m1, yunit="density", data="none", add=TRUE, 
     tline=list(col="red", lwd=2),
     cline=list(lty=0))

legend("topright", c("Offline", "HumanUse"), col=1:2, lty=1, lwd=2)
```

And perform the statistical test:

```{r ch9_16, class.source="Rmain"}
# Note reps reduced to speed up running time - people typically use 1000.
compareCkern(m1, m2, reps = 100)
```

Again, the observed overlap (0.83) is lower than we would expect if deer had the same activity pattern on both feature types (0.96), and none of the randomisations produced an overlap this low. This suggests the patterns differ, although they still overlap substantially, so the size of any change looks modest.

## Season comparisons

Every comparison so far pools all months of the year. Solar time stops the short winter day from squeezing dawn and dusk together, but it cannot tell us whether the animals themselves change their daily routine between seasons. If they do, a pooled curve hides it, and a pooled comparison between two species also mixes their seasons in whatever proportions they happened to be detected.

Let's label each detection by season: winter (November to March) and summer (May to August). We leave April, September and October out of the comparison.

```{r ch9_season_1, class.source="Rmain"}
img_locs$season <- "other"
img_locs$season[month(img_locs$timestamp) %in% c(11, 12, 1, 2, 3)] <- "winter"
img_locs$season[month(img_locs$timestamp) %in% 5:8] <- "summer"

# Images per season for our two species
table(img_locs$sp, img_locs$season)[c("Odocoileus.virginianus", "Rangifer.tarandus"), ]
```

The two species were detected in very different seasonal proportions: about a quarter of the deer images come from winter, but under a tenth of the caribou images do.

**White-tailed deer in winter and summer**

```{r ch9_season_2, class.source="Rmain"}
m_win <- fitact(img_locs$solar[img_locs$sp=="Odocoileus.virginianus" &
                                 img_locs$season=="winter"], sample="model", reps=100)
m_sum <- fitact(img_locs$solar[img_locs$sp=="Odocoileus.virginianus" &
                                 img_locs$season=="summer"], sample="model", reps=100)
```

```{r ch9_season_3, class.source="Rmain"}
compareCkern(m_win, m_sum, reps = 100)
```

**Caribou in winter and summer**

```{r ch9_season_4, class.source="Rmain"}
c_win <- fitact(img_locs$solar[img_locs$sp=="Rangifer.tarandus" &
                                 img_locs$season=="winter"], sample="model", reps=100)
c_sum <- fitact(img_locs$solar[img_locs$sp=="Rangifer.tarandus" &
                                 img_locs$season=="summer"], sample="model", reps=100)

compareCkern(c_win, c_sum, reps = 100)
```

Now let's plot them two ways. The top row compares the seasons within each species; the bottom row compares the species within each season. All four panels share the same y-axis, so the heights of their curves can be compared.

```{r ch9_season_5, class.source="Rmain", fig.width=9, fig.height=7}
# Draw two fitted curves in one panel. ylim is set by hand so every panel
# shares a scale tall enough for the tallest curve
two_curves <- function(a, b, cols, title) {
  plot(a, yunit="density", data="none", las=1, ylim=c(0, 0.3), main=title,
       tline=list(col=cols[1], lwd=2),
       cline=list(lty=0)) # Supress confidence intervals
  plot(b, yunit="density", data="none", add=TRUE,
       tline=list(col=cols[2], lwd=2),
       cline=list(lty=0))
}

par(mfrow = c(2, 2)) # two rows of two panels

# Top row: seasons within each species
two_curves(m_sum, m_win, c("black", "red"), "Deer: summer vs winter")
legend("top", c("Summer", "Winter"), col=c("black", "red"), lty=1, lwd=2,
       horiz=TRUE, bty="n", cex=0.8)
two_curves(c_sum, c_win, c("black", "red"), "Caribou: summer vs winter")

# Bottom row: species within each season
two_curves(m_sum, c_sum, c("darkorange", "blue"), "Summer: deer vs caribou")
legend("top", c("Deer", "Caribou"), col=c("darkorange", "blue"), lty=1, lwd=2,
       horiz=TRUE, bty="n", cex=0.8)
two_curves(m_win, c_win, c("darkorange", "blue"), "Winter: deer vs caribou")

par(mfrow = c(1, 1)) # back to one panel
```

On this axis, sunrise and sunset sit at the same place all year, at their average times across all the images (about 06:35 and 20:20), so read it as time relative to the sun rather than clock time.

In the top row, the deer curves overlap by only 0.52, against 0.96 expected if deer kept the same timing relative to sunrise and sunset all year. So they do not. But be careful about what that means. Solar time squeezes the long winter night into the same stretch of the axis as the short summer one, so even a deer that kept exactly the same clock-time routine all year would show winter and summer curves about this far apart. Comparing the seasons on clock time as well rules out that simplest alternative:

```{r ch9_season_6, class.source="Rmain"}
m_win_clock <- fitact(img_locs$clock[img_locs$sp=="Odocoileus.virginianus" &
                                       img_locs$season=="winter"], sample="model", reps=100)
m_sum_clock <- fitact(img_locs$clock[img_locs$sp=="Odocoileus.virginianus" &
                                       img_locs$season=="summer"], sample="model", reps=100)

compareCkern(m_win_clock, m_sum_clock, reps = 100)
```

On clock time the deer curves still overlap by only 0.66, against 0.95 expected for a fixed clock routine. So the deer keep neither the same clock routine all year nor the same place between sunrise and sunset. Overlap alone cannot say what they do instead: a deer that timed its whole day from dusk, the same way in every season, would fail both tests too. What the tests do show is that the pooled curve blends two different seasonal curves. In summer, the curve peaks after sunrise and in the evening. In winter, most of it falls in the long night. Read the broad shapes rather than the smaller bumps: a curve fitted to a limited number of events picks up wiggles that another year's data might not repeat.

The caribou panel (top right) looks even more dramatic than the deer. Its overlap (0.45) is lower still, and `pNull` says no randomisation came close. But its winter curve is built from very little: the bump near 18:00, for example, is a single visit ten frames long. Look at what the curve rests on:

```{r ch9_season_7, class.source="Rmain"}
cw <- img_locs[img_locs$sp=="Rangifer.tarandus" & img_locs$season=="winter", ]
c(images = nrow(cw), events = length(unique(cw$event_id)), sites = length(unique(cw$placename)))
```

Sixty-five images, but only 12 detection events at 6 sites. `compareCkern` builds its null by resampling single images, so it treats each frame of a burst as a separate observation. A fairer test keeps each event's images together: shuffle the season labels among *events* and see how often an overlap this low turns up by chance.

```{r ch9_season_8, class.source="Rmain"}
set.seed(9)
cs <- img_locs[img_locs$sp=="Rangifer.tarandus" & img_locs$season %in% c("winter", "summer"), ]
ev <- cs[!duplicated(cs$event_id), c("event_id", "season")] # one season per event

obs <- ovl4(fitact(cs$solar[cs$season=="winter"]), fitact(cs$solar[cs$season=="summer"]))

null <- replicate(100, {
  s <- sample(ev$season)[match(cs$event_id, ev$event_id)] # shuffle seasons among events
  ovl4(fitact(cs$solar[s=="winter"]), fitact(cs$solar[s=="summer"]))
})

c(observed = unname(obs), mean_null = mean(null), p = mean(null <= obs))
```

With only a dozen winter events, the curves of two random groups of events already overlap by about 0.5 on average, and an overlap as low as the observed one turns up in about a third of these shuffles (the share changes with the seed, but stays far above 5%). So the data do not show that caribou change their timing between seasons. Run the same test on the deer (swap the species in the chunk above) and their winter and summer curves differ well beyond chance, because their winter curve rests on many more events. When you split data into strata, always check how many *independent* events each curve rests on, not just how many images.

Now look back at the bottom row of the figure, which puts the two species side by side within each season. In summer both peak after sunrise and in the evening, but caribou become active well before sunrise, while deer stay more active through the afternoon. In winter they look very different, but that rests on the same 12 caribou events.

Three things follow for comparing activity patterns:

-   The deer vs caribou comparison mixes a deer sample that is about a quarter winter with a caribou sample that is under a tenth winter. Comparing species within one season, as in the bottom row of the figure, removes most of that difference in seasonal mix, though even within winter the caribou images come more from November than the deer images do.
-   The species and feature-type comparisons were tested with `compareCkern` too, so they rest on the same image-level null. Try the event shuffle above on them.
-   Seasonal comparisons are where the `tz` setting in `solartime()` matters most. If your cameras switch to daylight saving time and you use a single offset, the detections from part of the year sit an hour off the sun.


## On your own

Try your own species comparisons. Remember we have the following species:

```{r ch9_17, echo=F}
unique(img_locs$sp)
```

You can also try other categorical strata comparisons, we have:

`feature_type`

```{r ch9_18, echo=F}
table(locs$feature_type)
```

Try repeating a species or feature type comparison within a single season (`img_locs$season`), and test it with the event shuffle from the season comparisons. Most of the deer and caribou "winter" images are from November: try narrowing winter to December to February and see whether the deer result holds.

## Selected further reading

[Houngbégnon, Fructueux GA, et al. "Daily Activity Patterns and Co-Occurrence of Duikers Revealed by an Intensive Camera Trap Survey across Central African Rainforests." Animals 10.12 (2020): 2200.](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33255400/)

[Ross J, Hearn AJ, Johnson PJ, Macdonald DW (2013). Activity patterns and temporal avoidance by prey in response to Sunda clouded leopard predation risk. Journal of Zoology, 290(2), 96,106.](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jzo.12018)

[Azevedo FC, Lemos FG, Freitas-Junior MC, Rocha DG, Azevedo FCC (2018). Puma activity patterns and temporal overlap with prey in a human-modifed landscape at Southeastern Brazil." Journal of Zoology](https://zslpublications.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/jzo.12558)
